raw_text: The last glow of sunset faded behind the water tower, leaving the abandoned freight yard in a sea of deepening shadows. Leo put a hand on Sam's arm. "Stay low. We'll wait until it's fully dark before we get any closer." Sam nodded, his heart thumping against his ribs. They lay flat on the embankment, the chill of the steel rail seeping through their jackets. For a week they had heard the rumors. Trucks coming and going from the old yard late at night. No one knew why. "What do you think they're doing?" Sam whispered. "I don't know. But we're going to find out." Leo's voice was quiet but determined. A single light blinked on in the long, dark shape of the main warehouse. Then it went out. "Okay," Leo breathed. "Now." He slid down the gravelly slope, landing with a soft crunch. Sam was right behind him. They moved from the cover of one derelict boxcar to the next, ghosts in a graveyard of iron. The air smelled of rust and damp earth. Leo, who had spent a summer working on a farm, moved with a practiced silence that Sam envied. He pointed with a gloved hand. "There. By the main warehouse." A large canvas covered truck was parked near a loading bay, its engine silent. "No one's around," Sam whispered, his curiosity getting the better of his fear. "Maybe they're all inside." "Let's find a window," Leo suggested. They skirted a wide pool of black water and pressed themselves against the corrugated metal wall of the warehouse. It felt cold and slick with dew. Leo led the way, his sneakers making no sound on the packed dirt. He stopped at a grimy window, crusted with years of filth, and carefully wiped a small circle clean. He peered inside for a long moment, then motioned for Sam to look. Sam put his eye to the opening. He could see men inside, working by the light of a single bare bulb. They were loading wooden crates into the back of another truck, this one parked inside the warehouse itself. He couldn't hear what they were saying. "We need to get closer," he mouthed to Leo. Leo shook his head and pointed back the way they came. It was too risky. But Sam was impatient. He edged along the wall, heading for the corner of the building. He thought he might be able to hear them from the loading bay. He took another step, putting his weight down carefully. His foot came down on a loose stack of empty oil cans. The clatter they made was impossibly loud in the silence. It echoed through the yard like a gunshot. A cold dread trickled down Sam's spine. From inside the warehouse, the voices stopped. The light went out. "Run!" Leo hissed, grabbing his arm. But it was too late. A heavy side door slid open with a screech of rusty rollers and two figures burst out. One of them caught Sam in the beam of a heavy flashlight, blinding him. He felt a powerful hand clamp down on his shoulder. Leo didn't run. He turned back and launched himself at the second man, trying to knock him off balance. It was useless. A thick arm wrapped around his chest and lifted him off the ground. "Well, what have we here?" a low voice growled. They were shoved roughly into the warehouse. The door slid shut behind them, plunging them into near total darkness. "Just a couple of snooping kids," another voice said. "What do we do with them?" "Tie them up. We're almost done here anyway. They won't be going anywhere for a while." Rough hands forced Sam's arms behind his back. He felt a coarse rope bite into his wrists, then another was cinched around his ankles. A moment later, he was pushed into a small, windowless office and dumped onto the floor. He heard Leo grunt as he received the same treatment beside him. "What about their car?" "They're kids. They probably walked. Chuck them in the tool locker. They'll be fine until morning." The main door to the office creaked open. Sam felt himself being lifted and half carried, half dragged a few feet, then shoved into a cramped, dark space that smelled of oil and metal shavings. The metal door clanged shut, and a heavy bar dropped into place. The sound was horribly final. Footsteps receded, then the distant sound of a truck engine starting up. Then, silence. "You okay?" Leo's voice was a strained whisper in the blackness. "Peachy," Sam grumbled. "Just call me Houdini." He tried to wriggle his hands, but the knots were tight and expertly tied. "This is a mess." "At least we found out something," Leo said. "They're smugglers. I saw the markings on the crates." He was quiet for a moment. "My hands. They tied them in front of me. I think I can reach my feet." There was a soft scraping sound as Leo struggled. Sam's own shoulders ached from being pulled back. He could feel the rough texture of the rope against his skin, but there was no give at all. "I'm trying to find something sharp," Leo muttered. "The floor is all wood splinters." More scraping, followed by a grunt of effort. "Wait. There's a screw head sticking up from the floorboards. It's a little loose." Sam could hear the faint sound of rope rasping against metal. The sound went on for what felt like an hour. Sam's legs were starting to go numb. "Anything?" he whispered. "It's slow," Leo said, his voice tight with concentration. "But I think it's working. The rope is starting to fray. Just a little more." Suddenly, there was a soft snap. "I'm through one strand," Leo said, a note of triumph in his voice. "My hands are a little looser now. Let me see if I can get to the main knot." Sam held his breath, listening to the renewed sounds of his friend's struggle. He felt a surge of hope. Maybe they weren't going to wait for morning after all. Leo grunted again. "It's giving. I think I can get a finger under it."

The knot was tight, but it had a single loop he could get a finger into. Leo worked his index finger under the coarse fiber, wiggling it, pushing it. The rope was stiff and dry. It scraped his knuckle raw. Sam listened to the soft grunts and the rustle of cloth. His own arms ached, and his legs were pins and needles. He tried to shift his weight but the ropes held him fast.

"Almost," Leo breathed. The sound was tight in his throat. "It's slipping."

Sam held his own breath. He could hear the rope fibers straining. There was a sudden give, a loud rasp of rope pulling through rope.

"Got it," Leo said. It was a gasp of triumph. A moment later Sam heard the ropes fall away with a soft thud. Leo took a deep, shuddering breath. "My hands are numb."

"Can you stand?" Sam whispered.

"I think so." There was a rustling sound, then the creak of floorboards as Leo shifted his weight. "Okay. I'm on my knees. Now for you. Where are you?"

"Right here." Sam tried to make a noise, shuffling his feet.

He felt Leo's hands touch his shoulder, then move down his back. The darkness was so complete it was like being wrapped in velvet. Leo's fingers fumbled for the knots at Sam's wrists.

"Hold still," Leo said. "I can't see a thing. It's all by feel."

Sam felt the clumsy probing of Leo's numb fingers. It was slow, frustrating work. More than once a finger slipped and the knot seemed to tighten. Sam's shoulders screamed in protest.

"This is tied differently from mine," Leo muttered. "They must have known what they were doing."

"Just hurry," Sam urged. His voice was strained.

"I'm trying." Leo’s fingers found a loop. He began to worry at it, pulling and twisting. It felt like an eternity. Sam focused on the faint sounds, the scrape of fingernail on rope, Leo's quiet breathing. Finally, he felt a loosening. One loop gave way. Then another.

"There," Leo said. The ropes around Sam's wrists went slack. Blood surged back into his hands with a painful tingling. Leo moved to his feet. "Your ankles next."

Untying Sam's ankles was faster. In a moment he was free, rubbing his wrists, trying to work the feeling back into them. He stretched his arms carefully. Every joint seemed to protest.

"Okay," Sam whispered, getting to his knees. "We're loose. Now what?"

"Now we get out of this box," Leo replied. His voice was gaining its confidence back. "Feel around the walls. There has to be a weak spot. A loose hinge, maybe."

They began to explore the small space with their hands. It was a metal locker, cold and solid. The walls were smooth steel sheets, riveted together. The door was just as solid, with no give at all.

"The bar is on the outside," Sam said, running his hands over the door's seam. "We can't push it open."

"Keep looking," Leo said. "What's on the floor?"

Sam dropped to his hands and knees. The floor was covered in wood shavings, grease, and small, discarded bits of metal. His hand closed around something long and hard.

"What is it?" Leo asked.

"I think it's a file," Sam said. He felt its grated surface, its pointed tang. "A big one. A bastard file."

"Perfect," Leo said. "Bring it to the door. Let's see if we can pry with it."

Sam crawled to the door, the file clutched in his hand. "Where do I put it?"

"Find the crack between the door and the frame," Leo instructed. "Right near the bottom corner. There might be enough of a gap."

Sam felt for the seam. He found the corner and wedged the pointed end of the file into the tiny space. It barely went in.

"I've got it in," he whispered. "Now what?"

"Push on it. Try to lever the door outward. I'll push with you."

They both put their shoulders to the door and pushed. Sam grunted, putting all his weight behind the file. The metal groaned. The tip of the file scraped against the steel frame.

"It's not moving," Sam said, panting.

"Try to wedge it in further," Leo suggested. "Wiggle it."

Sam worked the file back and forth. The metal shrieked in protest. He managed to get another fraction of an inch into the crack.

"Okay, again," Leo said.

They pushed. This time there was a slight groaning sound from the doorframe. It wasn't much, but it was something.

"It moved!" Sam whispered excitedly. "I felt it give."

"Again," Leo urged.

They pushed again, and again. Each time the groan was a little louder. They worked in a rhythm, pushing, resting, then pushing again. The file was biting into the softer wood of the doorframe behind the metal. Splinters fell to the floor.

"The wood is giving way," Sam said. "We can do this."

They gave one more coordinated shove. There was a loud crack and the file suddenly plunged deeper. The bottom of the door bent outward an inch.

"We have a space," Leo said. "Is it enough?"

"I don't know." Sam tried to get his fingers into the gap. The edge of the steel was sharp. "We need to make it bigger."

"Use the file," Leo said. "Keep prying."

Sam worked the file up the side of the door, levering and pushing. The wood frame splintered and tore. The metal door skin began to buckle away from the frame. It was noisy work. Sam paused, listening.

"You think they can hear us?" he whispered.

"They're long gone," Leo said. "Keep going."

With a final, wrenching heave, a section of the door near the bottom corner bent out far enough for a person to squeeze through. It was a jagged, ugly hole.

"I think that's it," Sam said, breathing heavily. He was covered in sweat and grime.

"You first," Leo said. "Be careful of the edges."

Sam lay on his stomach and carefully began to worm his way through the opening. A sharp edge of torn metal snagged his jacket, ripping it. He twisted his body and pulled free, tumbling out onto the dusty floor of the office. He was out. He scrambled to his feet in the darkness.

"I'm through," he whispered back into the locker.

A moment later, Leo followed. He was just as grimy but grinning in the dark. "Step one complete," he said softly. "Now for the office door."

They felt their way to the office door. Sam's hand found the knob. He turned it. It was locked, just as they had expected.

"No luck," he said.

"Let me try," Leo said. "Maybe I can pick it. I need a piece of wire or something."

"Back in the locker?" Sam suggested.

"Good idea." Leo went back to the mangled locker door and felt around inside. After a moment he came back. "This will have to do." He held up a long, thin piece of metal. It looked like a feeler gauge.

Leo knelt at the door. Sam could hear the faint click and scrape as he inserted the thin strip of metal into the keyhole. It was an old, simple lock. Leo worked patiently, his head cocked as he listened. Sam stood guard, his ears straining for any sound from outside the office. The warehouse was silent as a tomb.

There was a soft click.

Leo grunted in satisfaction. "That's the first pin."

He continued to work, his movements small and precise. Sam was amazed. He had no idea his friend had such a skill.

"Where did you learn to do that?" he whispered.

"Read it in a book once," Leo said without looking up. "Never thought I'd actually need it."

Another click. And then another. Suddenly, with a louder clack, the mechanism turned. Leo slowly rotated the doorknob. The latch slid back. He pushed the door open a crack.

"We're in," he said, a note of awe in his own voice.

They peered out into the vast, dark space of the warehouse. A faint sliver of moonlight came from a high, grimy window, illuminating floating dust motes and the vague shapes of stacked crates. The air smelled of salt and diesel fuel.

"Okay," Sam whispered. "Let's see what they were so eager to hide."

They crept out of the office, moving slowly and deliberately. The main floor of the warehouse was filled with rows of large wooden crates. They were stacked high, creating narrow canyons between them.

"The ones I saw were over here," Leo whispered, pointing toward the back.

They made their way down an aisle of boxes. Leo stopped at a particular stack. "These are the ones. See the markings?"

Sam leaned closer. In the dim light he could make out a stenciled symbol. It was a stylized bird of prey inside a circle. Underneath it was a series of numbers and letters.

"What do you think it is?" Sam asked.

"I don't know. A company logo? A code?" Leo ran his hand over the rough wood of the nearest crate. "We need to see what's inside."

"How? We don't have a crowbar."

"We have a file," Leo reminded him. He pulled the big metal file from his belt. "Let's find a lid that looks loose."

They examined the crates. Most were nailed shut tightly. But one, on the top of a low stack, had a lid that seemed to be slightly pried up at one corner, as though someone had started to open it and been interrupted.

"This one," Sam said, pointing. "I can get my fingers under it."

"Give me a boost."

Sam laced his hands together and Leo stepped into them. Sam lifted, grunting with the effort. Leo scrambled onto the top of the lower crates and knelt beside the target box.

"Hand me the file," he said.

Sam passed it up. Leo inserted the tip of the file under the lid and began to pry. The wood creaked. Nails screeched as they were pulled from the wood. It was loud in the silent warehouse.

"Easy," Sam hissed.

"Can't be helped," Leo grunted.

With a final wrench, a section of the lid popped loose. Leo worked the file along the edge, and soon the entire lid was free. He pushed it aside.

"What is it?" Sam asked anxiously from the floor.

Leo was silent for a moment. He reached into the crate. "It's packed in straw. And there's some kind of foam padding." He pulled away the packing material. "Sam, you need to see this."

"What?"

"It's not what I expected," Leo said, his voice hushed. "It's not guns or drugs. It's... electronics. Really advanced-looking stuff."

He leaned down and passed a component to Sam. It was a metal box, cool to the touch, about the size of a book. It was covered in complex wiring and ports Sam didn't recognize. It was far too sophisticated for any normal commercial gear.

"This looks like military hardware," Sam said, turning it over in his hands. "Or something for aerospace."

"Exactly," Leo said from above. "This isn't simple smuggling. This is something else entirely."

Suddenly, a sound cut through the silence. The distinct noise of a car engine, slowing down, pulling up outside the warehouse. Then, the engine cut out.

"Someone's back," Sam breathed, his heart pounding.

"Get down!" Leo hissed. He scrambled off the crates, landing silently on the concrete floor. He pulled Sam into the narrow space between two tall stacks of crates.

"Did they see the light from the window?" Sam worried.

"No time. Just be quiet."

They pressed themselves against the rough wood, hidden in the deep shadows. The large rolling door of the warehouse rattled loudly as someone began to raise it. A rectangle of pale light spilled into the darkness, silhouetting a single man.

The man stepped inside. He left the door partly open. He pulled a small flashlight from his pocket and flicked it on. The narrow beam cut through the gloom, dancing across the crates.

"Stupid," the man muttered to himself. "Left the whole manifest."

He walked down the main aisle, his footsteps echoing in the huge space. Sam and Leo held their breath. The man was walking directly toward the office. He would have to pass their hiding spot.

The flashlight beam swept past them, just feet away. Sam squeezed his eyes shut, as if that would make him more invisible. The man continued to the office. He pushed the door open.

"What the..." the man's voice was sharp. He shone his light into the office, then on the mangled tool locker. "What happened here?"

Sam's blood ran cold. He knew they were caught.

The man swore under his breath. He swept his flashlight beam around the warehouse interior, more urgently this time. The light played over the stacks of crates, searching. It passed over their hiding spot once, twice. Then it stopped. The beam was pointed directly at the crate Leo had opened. The pried-off lid was clearly visible.

"No," the man whispered. He walked quickly toward the stack. He stood right in front of their hiding place, his back to them, and pointed his light into the open crate. Sam could have reached out and touched him.

The man let out a string of curses. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a radio.

"Jake, you there?" he said into it. The radio crackled to life.

"Yeah, what is it, Marco? You get the papers?"

"Forget the papers! The kids are gone. They broke out of the locker and they popped one of the crates. They know, Jake. They know what's in them."

There was a pause. The voice on the radio was grim. "Are they still there?"

"I don't see them. But the crate is still open. They can't have gone far." Marco swept his light around again, this time more methodically, aisle by aisle. "I'm telling you, they're here somewhere."

"Don't let them get out," the radio voice commanded. "I'm turning around. I'm five minutes away. Find them."

"Right," Marco said. He clicked the radio off.

He was no longer just looking. He was hunting. He began to move down the first aisle, his flashlight beam probing every shadow, every gap between the crates. Sam and Leo were trapped. There was nowhere to run. The aisle they were in was a dead end.

"What do we do?" Sam mouthed silently to Leo.

Leo's eyes were wide, but his mind was racing. He looked up. Above them, the crates were stacked almost to the ceiling, but there was a small gap between the top of the stack and the steel roof trusses. He pointed upward.

It was their only chance.

Marco was getting closer. They could hear his feet crunching on the dusty concrete.

Leo put a foot on a cross-brace of the crate in front of him. He found a handhold and began to climb, moving as silently as a cat. Sam followed right behind him. The old wood creaked ominously under their weight.

"What was that?" Marco's voice was sharp. He stopped moving.

Sam froze, halfway up the stack. He pressed his body flat against the crates, trying to become part of the shadow.

The flashlight beam shot down the aisle, illuminating the space just below Sam's feet. It held there for a long moment. Sam didn't dare breathe. Then, the beam moved on.

Marco must have decided it was a rat. He resumed his search in the next aisle over.

Leo was already at the top. He gestured for Sam to hurry. Sam scrambled the rest of the way up. They lay flat on top of the crates, their hearts hammering against their ribs. The roof was only a few feet above their heads.

Below, they could see the moving dot of Marco's flashlight as he searched the warehouse floor. They were exposed, but the deep shadows of the high ceiling offered some protection.

"He's going to check up here eventually," Leo whispered, his lips next to Sam's ear.

"We have to get out," Sam whispered back. "The high window."

He pointed toward the front of the warehouse. The grimy window that let in the moonlight was their only hope. But it was on the other side of the warehouse, and Marco was between them and it.

"We have to go over the top," Leo decided. "We can move from stack to stack."

It was a perilous idea. The tops of the crates were uneven, and a single misstep would send them crashing to the floor. But it was better than waiting to be found.

They began to crawl, moving with infinite slowness across the top of the crate stack. Below, Marco continued his search. He was being thorough.

They reached the end of their stack. The next one was five feet away. A dark chasm.

"I can make it," Leo whispered. "It's a long jump."

"You'll make too much noise," Sam argued.

Leo looked around. His eyes fell on a long, loose plank on top of their crate, probably left over from the packing. It was about eight feet long.

"A bridge," he breathed.

Together, they carefully lifted the plank. It was heavy and awkward. They slowly, carefully, pushed it out across the gap until it rested on the edge of the next stack. It seemed stable.

Leo went first. He crawled across the narrow plank, his weight making it bow precariously. Sam watched, his stomach in a knot. Leo made it to the other side. He gestured for Sam to follow.

Sam took a deep breath and started across. He kept his eyes on the other side, not daring to look down. The plank shifted under him. He froze. Below, Marco's light flickered as he moved out from an aisle. Sam flattened himself on the plank.

The light beam swept across the floor, then started to travel upward. It climbed the stack of crates directly across from them. Sam's heart stopped. Any second now, the beam would hit them.

Then they heard the sound of the truck again, this time pulling right up to the door. Brakes squealed. Doors slammed.

"Marco!" a voice yelled from the entrance. "Anything?"

"Nothing yet," Marco called back. "But they're here. I can feel it."

The distraction saved them. Marco lowered his beam and went to meet his partners at the door. Two more men entered the warehouse, both carrying powerful flashlights.

"Spread out," the one named Jake ordered. "Check every inch. They're just kids. They can't have vanished."

Now there were three of them searching.

"Go now," Leo urged.

Sam scrambled the rest of the way across the plank. They pulled it over after them and continued their desperate journey across the rooftops of the crates. They repeated the process twice more, bridging the gaps, crawling across, pulling their bridge after them.

Finally, they were on the stack of crates nearest the front of the warehouse. The high window was just ahead of them. It was a metal-framed factory window, coated with years of grime. One of the lower panes was cracked.

"That's our way out," Leo said.

They crept to the edge of the stack. The window was about ten feet away, and slightly above them. It was set into the concrete wall. There was a narrow steel beam running just below it.

"We have to jump to that beam," Sam said. The drop to the floor was at least twenty feet.

"No choice," Leo said. He looked back. The three beams of light were getting closer, sweeping across the floor and starting to move up the stacks. "I'll go first. If I make it, I'll help you."

Leo backed up to get a running start. It was only two steps. He leaped across the gap. His sneakers hit the steel beam with a soft thud. He windmilled his arms for balance, teetering on the narrow ledge. For a heart-stopping second, Sam thought he would fall. Then he found his balance and pressed himself flat against the wall.

"Come on," he hissed.

Sam took a breath and jumped. His feet hit the beam hard. His ankle twisted, and a sharp pain shot up his leg. He cried out, stifling the sound, and fell against the wall next to Leo.

"You okay?" Leo whispered.

"Twisted my ankle," Sam gritted his teeth against the pain. "I'm okay."

Below, one of the flashlight beams froze. "Hear that?" a man asked.

The beam shot upward, directly toward them. It caught Leo's foot.

"There they are!" the man yelled. "Up by the window!"

The other two beams converged on them, pinning them in the bright glare.

"No time," Leo said. He turned to the window and smashed the cracked pane with his elbow. The glass shattered and fell to the floor far below. "Go!"

He boosted Sam up toward the opening. Sam scrambled through, cutting his hands on the remaining shards of glass. He dropped onto a narrow ledge on the outside of the building. The night air was cold on his face. He turned and reached back for Leo.

Leo was already climbing through. Just as he pulled his legs free, a hand grabbed his ankle from inside.

"Got you!" Marco yelled.

Leo kicked backward, his heel connecting with a solid crunch. The man grunted in pain and his grip loosened. Leo pulled his leg free and tumbled out onto the ledge next to Sam.

"They're getting away!" a voice shouted from inside.

There was no time to think. They were on a narrow second-story ledge with no fire escape. But next to them, a thick electrical conduit ran down the side of the building.

"It'll have to do," Leo said. He swung his body over the ledge and grabbed onto the conduit. It was slick with grease and rain, but it held his weight. He began to slide down, his hands and shoes smoking from the friction.

Sam followed, his bad ankle screaming in protest. The conduit was rough and tore at his palms. He slid more than climbed, his descent clumsy and fast. He hit the ground hard, collapsing in a heap.

Leo was already on his feet, pulling him up. "Come on! To the car!"

They limped away from the warehouse, plunging into the darkness of the surrounding marshland. Behind them, they heard shouting and the warehouse door rolling all the way up.

"They're heading for the road!"

They ran, Sam leaning on Leo, his ankle throbbing with every step. They burst out of the reeds and onto the dirt track where they had hidden their old sedan.
